messages.body_plain:
Hi folks,
  Just wanted to let everyone know that the statnet team has released 
updates to most of the major statnet packages in the last week or so 
including some new features and a number of bug fixes.  You should be 
able to update everything to the most recent versions by installing the 
new "2016.4" version of the statnet package.

The ergm.ego and ergm.rank and statnetWeb packages have been released to 
CRAN as well.

best,
  -skye (for the statnet team)


Below are relevant excerpts from to the NEWS files for some of the packages:
----------------------------
ergm  version 3.6.0
NEW FEATURES

     A new suite of geometrically-weighted family of terms has been 
added that allow the user to specify what directions of shared 
partnerships are of interest. The new terms are,

         (Directed) geometrically weighted dyadwise shared partners (dgwdsp)

         (Directed) geometrically weighted edgewise shared partners (dgwesp)

         (Directed) geometrically weighted non-edgewise shared partners 
(dgwnsp)

     In addition, terms for specific shared partner counts (ddsp, desp, 
and dnsp) are also implemented. See ergm-terms for help.

     New terms (binary and valued) b1cov and b2cov have been 
implemented, analogous to nodecov, nodeicov, and nodeocov but for 
bipatite networks.

     New valued terms atleast, equalto, and smallerthan have been 
implemented. A number of terms that were binary-only before have been 
implemented for valued ERGMs.

     ergm package now works when loaded (e.g., using requireNamespace) 
but not attached (e.g., using library).

BUG FIXES

     A number of implementation bugs in the valued ERGM terms have been 
fixed.

     Parallel processing when using ergm.userterms and similar was 
accidentaly broken in the previous release.

     Calculation of Hummel et. al. (2010) steplength for missing data 
MLE was incorrect; a slower but more accurate algorithm is now used.

     Miscellaneous bugfixes and robustifications.

     gof.formula and others now work with missing data.

     Miscelaneous cleanups and bug fixes.

OTHER USER-VISIBLE CHANGES

     robust.inverse has been deprecated in favor of ginv.

     simulate.formula now does parallel processing more efficiently.

----------------------------

tergm  version 3.4.0
BUG FIXES

     Miscellaneous bugfixes.

     The list of functions exported is now explicitly defined.

     robust.inverse has been replaced by ginv.


-------------------

EpiModel Version 1.2.5

NEW FEATURES
* Added multicore functionality to simulating stochastic network models 
with `netsim`. This
   only supports single-node frameworks currently, using the 
`doParallel` package. Run models
   in parallel by using the `ncores` parameter in `control.net`.
* Modifications to the `as.phylo.transmat` function to construct the 
phylo tree with all
   network vertices as phylo-tips and all transmissions as phylo nodes.

OTHER
* General code cleanup and improvement of package tests to increase 
coverage about 90%.


---------------------------
ergm.count version 3.2.1
BUG FIXES

     Package now works when loaded but not attached.

     Test that was failing with ergm 3.6.0 has been fixed.

----------------------------
ndtv v0.9

  - added a jitter parameter to transmission timeline
  - fixed ndtv-d3 htmlwidget to correctly use a unique javascript id for 
the animation so that multiple animations can appear in the same 
Rmarkdown document
  - fixed warning and extra diagonal line drawn in timePrism plot when 
planes=TRUE and network had odd number of vertices.
  - updated MDSJ url to reflect changes at hosting server and correct 
CRAN error

----------------------------

tsna v 0.2
   - Added aggregate.dur parameters to the tErgmStats and tSnaStats 
wrapper functions so they can be used with networks having momentary ties
   - moved ergm package from Depends to Suggests now that ergm permits 
loading via requireNamespace

----------------------------

networkDynamic v0.9
   - vignette updates
   - fixed issue where network.collpase would incorrectly nest dynamic 
network-level attributes if there was only one of them
   - updated McFarland classroom networks to include TEA edge attributes
   - updated as.data.frame.networkDynamic() to mostly fix dramatic speed 
cost of filtering features from previous release, doc corrections
   - removed warning generated by as.data.frame.networkDynamic() when 
network has no edge activity to return

Dear Sebastian,

I have not used TERGMs yet so I cannot help you with this explicit error.
However, I have some serious concerns with this reasoning for using a TERGM
instead of SIENA. The working paper (I do not think the paper is a
published, peer reviewed article - please correct me if I am wrong), has
some serious flaws.

First: SAOMs are not a special case of a TERGM. Both are stochastic models
of networks but the SAOM only behaves like an ERGM in is long-run
equilibrium if a very, very unnatural and specific setting for the rate
function is used. In virtually all real world applications, it does
not. Also, unlike the ERGM, the SAOM is not typically used to analyse
networks in equilibrium. The TERGM, however, is special case of an ERGM -
an ERGM conditioned on another network.

Second: Some (Most?) of the critique IN THE ARXIV PAPER against SAOMs is
equally valid against (T)ERGMs:
a) It is absolutely true that SAOMs have problems capturing joint actions,
as common in politics (i.e. formation of the European Union), but the same
type of emergence is, as far as I know, hard to model in (T)ERGMs. It would
require a clique effect, which I have not encountered and I think does not
exists. SAOMs probably should not be used for joint action networks, but
this does not apply for your data. (I assume that the primates you study
behave somewhat like small human social networks.)
b) Of course it is unnatural to assume that every single actor has the
exact same objective function. But the same is true for a (T)ERGM. In a
SAOM we assume that our parameters model the average decision of the
average person (given its network position and covariates), in an ERGM we
assume our parameters capture the formation of an average tie (given its
network position and covariates). If we do not specify a specific subgroup
(i.e. by interacting a parameter with a co-variate like gender), both TERGM
and SAOM assume that processes are similar for all members of the network
(given their position in it). The (T)ERGM in fact makes stronger
homogeneity assumptions because not only actors but even all tie variables
follow the same probabilistic rules!
c) Another critique is that SAOMs assume that everyone is aware of the
whole network state, when they make a decision. As before it is clear that
this assumption is unnatural, especially in larger networks. But in a
(T)ERGM the probability of a tie is also dependent on the existence of
other ties in the network. In terms of information needed, the TERGM and
the SAOM are no different - only most TERGM papers are silent about this
complete information assumption, while SAOM papers are more often open
about it.

Third: The simulation part of the paper in section 5 uses quite "weird"
parameters to compare the model families. Choosing random draws from a
uniform distribution of -3 to +3 with steps of .001 does not lead to
meaningful parameters for neither a TERGM nor SAOM. The resulting networks
will be mostly degenerate or at least will not look like your average
social network. A simulation should be based on target statistics of a
network.

What I wanted to say is, that the paper has flaws. I am not a
mathematically trained statistician, like the inventors of ERGMs, TERGMs
and SAOMs so I am sure that I have some inaccuracies in the way that I
wrote things down here and I would love to hear what the statnet authors
and other statisticians/mathematicians or more knowledgeable people have to
say about this paper. But I am quite sure that SIENA is not a bad choice
for the type of network you are dealing with. Additionally, if the results
of TERGM and SAOM differ, I would not know what that meant.


A positive thing in SAOMs is that the parameters are time
independent because it is a continuous time model (TERGM is discrete-time).
If you observe the same network at  multiple points in time and the
underlying process is constant, then the parameter estimates of the SAOMs
should be the same for T1-T2-T3 compared to T1-T3. Or if the time intervals
are of different length (e.g. First measurements apart by 2 months and
later by 6 months). If your model is well fitting and the process is
stable, the parameters will be the same, because it is a model of
individual decisions. The same does not hold TERGMs, as far as I know.

I want to emphasize that I do not think that TERGMs are worse than SAOM.
They are different mathematical models with different goals. One is
modelling the state of a network given a previous time point and one models
the process of change. If your interest is in how behavior and social
relations of primates co-evolve, SAOMs should work fine. If you are
interested in how the structure of your primate group is, conditioned on a
previous observation, than TERGMs are the model for you.

I am sorry that I cannot help you with your errors, but I wanted to
re-assure you that your SIENA results could be sufficient after all.


Best Regards,

Robert Krause

ICS Sociology, PhD Student
University of Groningen
Grote Rozenstraat 31,
Room B119
9712 TG Groningen, The Netherlands

This seems to be an old thread. I don't know if Sebastian already
received some answer off the list... Nevertheless:

@Sebastian, regarding the error messages. I presume the data is an
undirected network. One thing I notice immediately is that you
included Sex and Matrilines node-level variables in both nodefactor
and nodecov terms. This is redundant as nodefactor and nodecov are
analogous and the only difference is that nodefactor treats the node
attribute as categorical while nodecov treats it as a continuous
variable. The difference is analogous to representing an effect of
some X in linear regression either (1) as is with beta*X or (2) as a
set of dummy variables with own beta's. I think this is the reason for
the "MCMLE estimation stuck. There may be excessive correlation
between model terms" error as both terms are probably linear functions
of each other. I am not sure about the origin of the first two errors,
but it may very well be that they are a consequence of the first
error.

@Robert, thanks for a very interesting summary!! I will be very
interested to read statnet-core members take on it. Meanwhile, can you
point me to a paper/publication based on which you wrote your first
comment about the ERGM vs SAOM and long-run equilibrium and rate
specification assumptions? I would really like to educate myself in
that respect.

Best,
Michal

Hey,

I am sorry for reviving the thread, but I did see that Sebastian got any
reply.

The authors of the working paper in question made the claim that SAOMs are
a special case of TERGMs referring to Snijders 2001. And indeed Snijders
2001 (referring to Snijders & van Duijn 1997) shows that if you take a very
specific, unnatural, setting for the rate function you obtain Wassermann's
reciprocity model (1979) -  see:
https://www.stats.ox.ac.uk/~snijders/sie_the.pdf page 22. This, however,
does not imply that any other (realistic) SAOM behaves like a (realistic)
ERGMs. Wassermann's reciprocity model is not a well fitting model for most
social networks either. It only shows that there is a mathematical
intersection of both model families.

Best Regards,

Robert Krause

University of Groningen

Room B119

Hello Jesse-

Alas, it sounds like you have discovered the wonders of model degeneracy 
-- that is, you've specified a model where even the true maximum 
likelihood estimates for the model would be so unlikely to produce the 
observed network that the estimation algorithm is unable to converge. 
This is a challenge with network models, where the intuition we bring 
from simple linear models is often confounded by the complex dependence 
in our data and among our model terms. And unlike in linear world, where 
starting with a simple model and building complexity is generally 
guaranteed to work, here a simple model can often be the source of the 
problem, because it doesn't capture the real-world processes that offset 
one another to prevent our social worlds from going off in one direction 
or another.

You might find it useful to go through the ERGM tutorial if you haven't 
before, and see the advice we give for diagnosing degeneracy:

https://statnet.org/trac/wiki/Sunbelt2016#WorkshopMaterials

You could also read up a lot more in depth on the statistical 
underpinnings of degeneracy if you wish, using resources pointed to on 
the statnet wiki.  I suspect your more immediate concern is finding a 
model that fits - and this group has a lot of built-up knowledge that 
they may offer.  I'd start by suggesting the use of degree terms instead 
of star terms; there is a direct mapping from one to the other, but the 
degree terms are generally far more stable; they're also easier for most 
readers to interpret If you wish to stay with stars, you might consider 
reading up about alternating k-stars.

Note that as you progress you might experience similar issues with your 
triangle term - if so, I'd suggest reading up about GWESP.

Cheers,
Steve

The problem is not with ERGMs per se - the problem is that you chose a 
model that was ill-suited to your system.  Poor specification is a 
problem in any context; try e.g. putting multiple high-order polynomial 
terms in a typical OLS and see how that goes.  Of course, learning how 
to specify better models takes some reading, and some practice, so one 
should not be surprised if one's first efforts go poorly.  (And the 
field as a whole is continuing to learn about how to specify improved 
models for different applications...it's a very active area.)  But the 
bottom line is that parametric modeling of an entire social network is a 
challenging problem that requires some expertise (!), and software tools 
can't substitute for that. Learning is required.

Vis a vis permutation methods, there are many clever things that can be 
done with those approaches.  They do, however, have a lot of intrinsic 
limitations, and are never going to be a general-purpose substitute for 
full probability models.  (By turns, there are things that you can do 
very easily and robustly with permutation techniques that are very hard 
to do in other ways.  As always, one wants to pick the right tool for 
the job.)

-Carter

Hi John,

I would say the disrespect actually started with your comment that ERGMs 
are not very useful.

But sniping is not useful here in any case.  We're actually all trying to 
understand how to represent systems with the types of dyad dependence 
you're talking about.  Constructive debate is part of that.

The issues with the homogenous reduced Markov model (which is a specific 
ERGM, but not the class of ERGMs) have been known for a long time.  The 
best way to understand it is as Steve G noted earlier:  this model does 
not generally produce interesting networks, *for any values of the 
parameters*.  So yes, this specific model are not very useful for 
empirical work.

But it's worth understanding why.  ERGMs are stochastic models, not just a 
descriptive summary of statistics you want to explore in your graph.  So 
if your goal is just to test whether the number of triangles is more or 
less than you would expect given the size and density of the graph, a CUG 
test is a perfectly good tool.  But if you want to understand the nature 
of the generative stochastic process that would lead to the graph you 
have, then you'll need an ERGM.  The fact that the homogenous reduced 
Markov model doesn't produce interesting graphs is indicative of model 
misspecification:  it's the wrong model for your graph.  And, as much 
research has shown, it's the wrong model for almost any sparse graph of 
reasonable size. (sparse here in the technical sense of < 50% density)

Since the word "generative" has also stimulated some controversy in the 
context of non-temporal ERGMs, let me say what I mean in this context. 
Generative in the sense that we can simulate realizations of networks from 
the distribution that this model defines, so we can see what the model 
implies about the networks it would produce. And generative and in the 
sense that looking at the conditional logit form allows you to interpret 
the coefficients in terms of the conditional log odds of a tie being 
present, given the other network statistics in the model.

There are lots of interesting technical reasons why the homogenous reduced 
Markov model "don't work".  It's hard to boil down to an email, but it's 
worth understanding.

Turning the question around, I'm not sure why you would want to put both 
gwesp and triangle terms in a model (did I misunderstand you?).  They 
would be so highly correlated they would make for a very unstable model, 
and even if you could get it to fit, I'm not sure I would be able to 
interpret the coefficients, would you?

Offered in the spirit of civil discussion ...

best,
mm

Hi, John -

You asked for our opinions on the issue of degeneracy, and you obtained 
one: (1) building good models in any complex system is a challenging 
task that requires knowledge of how the model class operates; (2) ERGMs 
are no exception; and (3) if you put together a bad model (e.g. the 
example that was offered) you will get poor results.  My comments 
regarding the necessity of learning and practice were made in response 
to your own claims to be a newcomer, your evident concern at the 
behavior of a very well-studied model class (see, e.g. Snijders's 2002 
JoSS paper for details on the edge/k-star family), and your apparent 
concern that failure to obtain a good model on a first try implies that 
the whole approach is broken.  I would be inclined to take those 
comments positively - i.e., this _is_ a learnable task, and indeed there 
are many exciting and intriguing things to discover - but they are 
relating a basic fact that you can celebrate or decry as you choose.

Substantively, Steve and Martina have made some very excellent comments 
on the modeling issues, which underscore some of the things to which one 
needs to attend in building good models.  The many threads in the 
current literature regarding model parameterization are an outgrowth of 
these important and hard-won lessons, and to understand this new work it 
is likewise necessary to know something about the foundational 
challenges that all such modeling efforts face.  (This knowledge is also 
important for sorting out the sometimes dubious claims that are made 
regarding what constitutes an "extension" or a fundamentally alternative 
approach - caveat emptor.)  These are as much substantive theoretical 
challenges as they are technical ones, as Martina, Steve, and many 
others have frequently emphasized: "bad" models generate unrealistic 
behavior because they posit social mechanisms that are themselves 
unrealistic.  As with any complex system, determining what is 
unrealistic in a network model is not trivial, and indeed we are 
learning quite a lot about the social world by studying "bad' models and 
mechanisms!  (I cut my teeth as an agent-based modeler, and my view was 
always that one learned more from the models that failed than from the 
ones that succeeded: there are lots of "obvious" ways to construct a 
system with specified behavior that do not in fact behave as you expect, 
usually for reasons that are clear only after one has banged one's head 
against the proverbial or actual table many times.)  To take the example 
of the edge/k-star/triangle family (which you raised), there were many 
plausible a priori arguments that suggested that such families would 
provide a good characterization of many classes of social networks.  
(See, e.g., the classic dependence arguments of Frank and Strauss 
(1986), although the thread goes back farther than that.)  When it was 
discovered that these models tended to be ill-behaved (a phenomenon of 
which Strauss himself warned in his 1986 SIAM paper), this meant that 
the underlying theoretical rationale for those models - that is, the 
ideas about how, when, and how strongly one edge could affect another - 
had to be revisited.  This has led to a whole slew of interesting 
proposals for alternative specifications, each of which is based on a 
substantively different notion of the mechanisms behind triangulation.  
This represents theoretical progress: the early models helped us learn 
that the world didn't work as we naively expected, and we are now 
investigating other ways that the world might work (with those proposals 
being guided by what we learned from the initial effort).  As of right 
now, it appears that there are several classes of factors that act in 
the real world to inhibit phenomena such as the density explosion, 
including (1) decoupling of edges across social or physical barriers, 
(2) heterogeneity in opportunity structures, and (3) diminishing 
marginal effects of closure on edge formation.  The jury is still out on 
exactly where, when, and how much these factors are active, but I expect 
that we will know more in the coming years as more models get tried, 
more/better data is acquired, and the properties of different 
specifications become better understood.  It's an exciting time to be in 
the field.

Hopefully, the above provides further elaboration of why familiarizing 
oneself with some background information is important for making 
progress with ERGMs (or any other modeling approach), and why I and 
others typically give this advice to newcomers.  It's natural to wander 
into the field, throw together some models that seem intuitively 
sensible (or are mentioned in old papers or more recent papers studying 
pathological models), and accidentally rediscover degeneracy.  This can 
be a useful learning experience (I suggest that everyone play with such 
models!) but can be frustrating if your proximate objective is getting a 
good model for some substantive purpose.  There's nothing unique about 
ERGMs in this regard; for instance, when I first started dabbling in 
molecular dynamics (and I'm still a neophyte in that domain), it took me 
a while to figure out that my proteins kept unfolding because I hadn't 
properly specified the disulfide bonds that were stitching them together 
(oops).  The model wasn't wrong per se - it was predicting what would 
really happen if those bonds got reduced - but it certainly wasn't doing 
what I intended.  (Ditto for getting protonation states right, something 
which can require some significant homework.)  In my experience, most 
folks readily expect that they will need to learn about such things to 
model physical systems, but some are surprised that modeling social 
networks also requires one to develop a deeper understanding of the 
underlying technical and substantive issues.  Indeed, this is the case.  
The good news, however, is that there _is_ more to learn than there was 
say, 15 years ago.  The science continues to advance.

Ultimately, you should choose the right tool for your problem, and that 
tool might or might not be a stochastic network model in ERGM form.  If 
you elect to work with the latter, the discussion and references posted 
here will hopefully provide you with information that can help you get 
started in this rich and fascinating research area.

Hope that helps,

-Carter

And just in case Carter's answer isn't long enough for you :)

It's worth making a distinction between the general form of the Markov 
model, and the homogeneous reduced form that most folks are familiar with.

The general specification allows for each configuration (edge, k-star or 
triangle) to have it's own coefficient.  That model is not identifiable. 
In fact, you run out of degrees of freedom on the edges terms alone, since 
each edge would have its own coefficient.

Hence the "simpler" 3 parameter model we've come to know and hate:  the 
edges+2star+triangle model.  It imposes both homogeneity constraints (each 
configuration now has a single coefficent, node labels don't matter 
anymore) and a reduced form from k-stars to 2-stars.

This homogenous reduced form Markov is, we now know, just a bad model. 
It doesn't produce interesting graphs, and it wouldn't produce any of the 
networks we're likely to analyze. Frank and Strauss committed the original 
sin, but the entire field is still learning this lesson.

But I don't think that means the Markov class as a whole is bad.  The 
heterogeniety is there in the class to exploit.  But the way to do it is 
with other effects, like homophily, that introduce interpretable 
heterogeneity into the configurations, and declining marginal returns (as 
Carter notes).

best,
mm

And to continue the riff further, I'd even say that the homogeneous 
Markov families have turned out to be very _good_ models for advancing 
ERGM theory: they are our go-to workhorses for studying challenges 
relating to mixing, phase transitions/degeneracy, and a host of other 
important problems.  Some of them also work well on very small networks 
(where the assumptions underlying them are more plausible).  So I'd 
personally exonerate Frank and Strauss of any particular sins on this 
issue: they made an important step forward both in showing that the 
triangle effects proposed by Holland and Leinhardt (in a part of their 
p1 paper that everyone forgets) could be estimated and in showing how 
both degree distribution bias and triangulation were inherently related 
to the Markov graph dependence structure.  We have since learned a lot 
about what needs to be done to build on those early insights and make 
them practical for complex networks in the real world (and we are still 
learning!), but this in no way diminishes their contributions.  IMHO.  :-)

-Carter

On 04/24/2016 05:18 PM, martina morris wrote:
> And just in case Carter's answer isn't long enough for you :)
>
> It's worth making a distinction between the general form of the Markov 
> model, and the homogeneous reduced form that most folks are familiar 
> with.
>
> The general specification allows for each configuration (edge, k-star 
> or triangle) to have it's own coefficient.  That model is not 
> identifiable. In fact, you run out of degrees of freedom on the edges 
> terms alone, since each edge would have its own coefficient.
>
> Hence the "simpler" 3 parameter model we've come to know and hate:  
> the edges+2star+triangle model.  It imposes both homogeneity 
> constraints (each configuration now has a single coefficent, node 
> labels don't matter anymore) and a reduced form from k-stars to 2-stars.
>
> This homogenous reduced form Markov is, we now know, just a bad model. 
> It doesn't produce interesting graphs, and it wouldn't produce any of 
> the networks we're likely to analyze. Frank and Strauss committed the 
> original sin, but the entire field is still learning this lesson.
>
> But I don't think that means the Markov class as a whole is bad. The 
> heterogeniety is there in the class to exploit.  But the way to do it 
> is with other effects, like homophily, that introduce interpretable 
> heterogeneity into the configurations, and declining marginal returns 
> (as Carter notes).
>
> best,
> mm

> On Apr 24, 2016, at 8:18 PM, martina morris <morrism@u.washington.edu> wrote:
> 
> And just in case Carter's answer isn't long enough for you :)
> 
> It's worth making a distinction between the general form of the Markov model, and the homogeneous reduced form that most folks are familiar with.
> 
> The general specification allows for each configuration (edge, k-star or triangle) to have it's own coefficient.  That model is not identifiable. In fact, you run out of degrees of freedom on the edges terms alone, since each edge would have its own coefficient.
> 
> Hence the "simpler" 3 parameter model we've come to know and hate:  the edges+2star+triangle model.  It imposes both homogeneity constraints (each configuration now has a single coefficent, node labels don't matter anymore) and a reduced form from k-stars to 2-stars.
> 
> This homogenous reduced form Markov is, we now know, just a bad model. It doesn't produce interesting graphs, and it wouldn't produce any of the networks we're likely to analyze. Frank and Strauss committed the original sin, but the entire field is still learning this lesson.
> 
> But I don't think that means the Markov class as a whole is bad.  The heterogeniety is there in the class to exploit.  But the way to do it is with other effects, like homophily, that introduce interpretable heterogeneity into the configurations, and declining marginal returns (as Carter notes).
> 
> best,
> mm

>> in any complex system is a challenging task that requires knowledge of how the model class operates;
>> (2) ERGMs are no exception; and (3) if you put together a bad model (e.g. the example that was offered)

>> well-studied model class (see, e.g. Snijders's 2002 JoSS paper for details on the edge/k-star family),

>> learnable task, and indeed there are many exciting and intriguing things to discover - but they are
>> relating a basic fact that you can celebrate or decry as you choose.
>> Substantively, Steve and Martina have made some very excellent comments on the modeling issues, which
>> underscore some of the things to which one needs to attend in building good models.  The many threads
>> in the current literature regarding model parameterization are an outgrowth of these important and
>> hard-won lessons, and to understand this new work it is likewise necessary to know something about the
>> foundational challenges that all such modeling efforts face.  (This knowledge is also important for

>> fundamentally alternative approach - caveat emptor.)  These are as much substantive theoretical
>> challenges as they are technical ones, as Martina, Steve, and many others have frequently emphasized:

>> reasons that are clear only after one has banged one's head against the proverbial or actual table many

>> plausible a priori arguments that suggested that such families would provide a good characterization of
>> many classes of social networks.  (See, e.g., the classic dependence arguments of Frank and Strauss
>> (1986), although the thread goes back farther than that.)  When it was discovered that these models
>> tended to be ill-behaved (a phenomenon of which Strauss himself warned in his 1986 SIAM paper), this
>> meant that the underlying theoretical rationale for those models - that is, the ideas about how, when,

>> interesting proposals for alternative specifications, each of which is based on a substantively

>> factors that act in the real world to inhibit phenomena such as the density explosion, including (1)
>> decoupling of edges across social or physical barriers, (2) heterogeneity in opportunity structures,
>> and (3) diminishing marginal effects of closure on edge formation.  The jury is still out on exactly

>>> It's worth making a distinction between the general form of the 
>>> Markov model, and the homogeneous reduced form that most folks are 
>>> familiar with.
>>>
>>> The general specification allows for each configuration (edge, 
>>> k-star or triangle) to have it's own coefficient.  That model is not 
>>> identifiable. In fact, you run out of degrees of freedom on the 
>>> edges terms alone, since each edge would have its own coefficient.
>>>
>>> Hence the "simpler" 3 parameter model we've come to know and hate: 
>>>  the edges+2star+triangle model.  It imposes both homogeneity 
>>> constraints (each configuration now has a single coefficent, node 
>>> labels don't matter anymore) and a reduced form from k-stars to 2-stars.
>>>
>>> This homogenous reduced form Markov is, we now know, just a bad 
>>> model. It doesn't produce interesting graphs, and it wouldn't 
>>> produce any of the networks we're likely to analyze. Frank and 
>>> Strauss committed the original sin, but the entire field is still 
>>> learning this lesson.
>>>
>>> But I don't think that means the Markov class as a whole is bad. 
>>>  The heterogeniety is there in the class to exploit.  But the way to 
>>> do it is with other effects, like homophily, that introduce 
>>> interpretable heterogeneity into the configurations, and declining 
>>> marginal returns (as Carter notes).

>>>> decoupling of edges across social or physical barriers, (2) 
>>>> heterogeneity in opportunity structures,

>>>> where, when, and how much these factors are active, but I expect 
>>>> that we will know more in the coming
>>>> years as more models get tried, more/better data is acquired, and 
>>>> the properties of different
>>>> specifications become better understood. It's an exciting time to 
>>>> be in the field.

>>>> information is important for making progress with ERGMs (or any

>>>> others typically give this advice to newcomers.  It's natural to

>>>> studying pathological models), and accidentally rediscover

>>>> objective is getting a good model for some substantive purpose.

>>>> this regard; for instance, when I first started dabbling in

>>>> neophyte in that domain), it took me a while to figure out that my

>>>> hadn't properly specified the disulfide bonds that were stitching

>>>> wasn't wrong per se - it was predicting what would really happen if

>>>> certainly wasn't doing what I intended. (Ditto for getting

>>>> can require some significant homework.) In my experience, most

Dear listserv members,

I'm trying to test a hypothesis about tie strength and similarity of
cultural attitudes (i.e., the stronger the tie between nodes, more similar
their attitudes would be).
I have tie strength as edge value (range 0-6), and cultural attitudes
measured with 5-point scale (so 1-5).
I'm using ergm terms like edgecov and nodematch to test that, and used
reference = ~Binomial(6). Am I doing it right?
Although the model did not converge, I'm getting most parameters
significant and very low AIC and BIC values.

Also, when I got this message "MCMLE estimation did not converge after 20
iterations. The estimated coefficients may not be accurate. Estimation may
be resumed by passing the coefficients as initial values; see 'init' under
?control.ergm for details." I tried to increase the sample size and
interval, but seemed to keep getting the same message. Can anyone tell me
what I can do better? or should I give up since it's a model degeneracy?

My network visualization (attached below) gave me some confidence about the
hypothesis, but maybe I'm doing something wrong.

Your advice/help will be greatly appreciated.

Sunny

I am still trying to figure out the error problem following the tutorial of the Sunbelt 2015 workshop https://statnet.org/trac/raw-attachment/wiki/Sunbelt2015/ergmEgo_tutorial.html <https://statnet.org/trac/raw-attachment/wiki/Sunbelt2015/ergmEgo_tutorial.html> , I found that if the data was extracted from the original ?faux.mesa.high? network object, and was directly used by the ergm.ego(), then no error occurred. The error did not show in the tutorial because the following analyses were based on the data extracted directly from the ?faux.mesa.high?, not on the data files exported and read back in.

So my questions is, what kind of data format does the ergm.ego() requires? The descriptive statistics worked fine for both $egos and $alters part, so I guess something went wrong when the egos part and alters part were connected (probably the two parts were not connected). Could you give me some suggestions please? What do I miss on the tutorial?

Thank you very much.

Ya
